God's glory appears among the exiles

The vision comes in Babylon, far from the temple. The throne has wheels that move in any direction (verse 17). So God’s presence is not fixed to one place. Verse 28 describes what Ezekiel saw with great caution. It was “the appearance of the likeness” of the LORD’s glory. He does not claim to describe God directly. The rainbow in the storm recalls the sign of mercy in Genesis 9:13.
Speaking does not depend on a willing audience

God calls Ezekiel “son of man,” which means a human being. The title follows directly on the vision of glory. Verse 2 says the Spirit had to set him on his feet. Verse 7 defines his task. He must speak whether the people hear or refuse. His success is not measured by their response. Verse 5 names the one sure result: they will know a prophet was there.
The messenger must hear before he warns

A watchman stood on the wall and warned of danger. Verse 17 puts hearing before warning. Ezekiel must first receive the word from God’s mouth. Verses 18–21 hold him responsible for giving the warning. They do not hold him responsible for the result. A watchman who keeps silent shares the guilt. Verse 26 adds that he will speak only what he is given.
A model siege reaches the prophet's body

Ezekiel does not only speak about the siege. For more than a year his own body lives on siege rations. His bread is weighed, and his water is measured (verses 10–11). The mixed grains of verse 9 suggest the last scraps of a store. Verse 16 explains the sign. Jerusalem will eat by weight and drink in fear. Verse 14 records the priest’s protest, and verse 15 grants a change.
Divided hair shows different forms of loss

The law told priests not to shave their heads (Leviticus 21:5). Ezekiel the priest does so with a sword. The hair is weighed on scales, so the judgment is measured. Verse 12 explains the three parts: disease and hunger, sword, and scattering. Verses 3–4 add a detail about the few hairs kept in his robe. Some of those are burned as well. Being among the survivors is no guarantee.
Ruined shrines become places of remembrance

Verse 9 says something unusual about God. He says he has been broken by their unfaithful hearts. The verse describes hurt as well as anger. It also gives survival a purpose. Those who escape will remember him and loathe their own acts. The chapter repeats “you will know that I am the LORD” four times. Surviving is meant to lead to knowing.
Wealth loses its power when daily life breaks

Verses 12–13 describe a market that has lost its meaning. Buying and selling land no longer matters. Verse 19 then says what happens to money. People throw it away as something unclean. It cannot rescue them, and it cannot feed them. The verse calls their wealth their stumbling block. Verse 20 explains: they made their gold into idols.
A vision exposes what elders claim is hidden

The elders in verse 12 hold two beliefs. The LORD does not see, and he has left the land. The vision itself answers the first. God shows Ezekiel what they do in the dark, each in his own room. The second belief is nearly true, for a reason they miss. Verse 6 says their acts are driving him from his sanctuary. The chapter moves through four scenes, each called worse than the last.
Grief distinguishes people within the city

Verse 4 says who receives the protecting mark. They are people who sigh and cry over what is done in the city. They could not stop it, and they did not accept it. Grief is what sets them apart. Verse 6 says the judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the elders. Ezekiel pleads for the people in verse 8. He does not watch in silence.
The glory leaves the sanctuary in stages

The glory leaves the temple in steps. It moves from the inner room to the threshold (9:3). In verse 18 it moves from the threshold to the cherubim. Verse 19 takes it to the east gate, and 11:23 to the hill beyond. The slow exit reads like reluctance. Verses 15 and 20 say these are the creatures Ezekiel saw in Babylon. What leaves Jerusalem is what appeared among the exiles.
The exiles receive a promise denied by city leaders

Verse 15 quotes Jerusalem’s residents about the exiles. They are far from the LORD, and the land now belongs to those who stayed. Verse 16 gives God’s reply. He himself has been a sanctuary to the exiles for a while. His presence did not depend on the building. Verse 19 then promises them a new heart of flesh. The people written off as rejected receive the promise.
The prophet's baggage challenges postponed warnings

Ezekiel acts first and explains only when asked (verse 9). Verse 11 gives the meaning: “I am your sign.” What he did will be done to them. The chapter quotes two sayings of the people. One says every vision fails (verse 22). The other says the vision is for a time far off (verse 27). A man carrying exile baggage today answers both.
False peace resembles a weak wall under plaster

Verse 5 says what a prophet should do. He should stand in the gap and repair the wall. Verse 10 shows what these prophets do. The people put up a thin wall of their own hopes. The prophets paint it white so that it looks sound. Verse 11 says a storm will test it. Verse 22 names the damage: the righteous lose heart and the wicked do not turn.
Another person's righteousness cannot replace one's own response

Verse 14 names three men known for righteousness. In their own stories each one helped others. Noah’s family entered the ark with him, and Job prayed for his friends. Here they could rescue no one else. Verses 16, 18, and 20 repeat it: not even sons or daughters. A person cannot rest on someone else’s goodness. The point is made four times, once for each disaster.
The burned vine offers no useful timber

Israel is often called a vine and praised for its fruit (Psalm 80:8–11). Ezekiel says nothing about fruit. He asks only about the wood. Vine wood is soft and twisted and makes nothing useful. A vine that bears no fruit has nothing else to offer. Verse 4 says the fire has already burned both ends. The short parable removes any pride in being God’s vine.
Jerusalem's story overturns its claims of superiority

Verse 49 defines Sodom’s guilt in social terms. She had pride, plenty of food, and easy comfort. She did not help the poor and needy. Verses 48 and 51 say Jerusalem has done worse. The comparison takes away her sense of being better. Verse 53 goes further and promises to restore Sodom too. The mercy of verses 60–63 is meant to leave her humbled.
The eagles explain a broken royal oath

The first eagle is Babylon, and the second is Egypt. Judah’s king swore loyalty to Babylon and then turned to Egypt. Verse 15 asks whether a man who breaks a covenant can escape. Second Chronicles 36:13 says the oath was sworn by God. In verse 19 God calls it “my oath.” A promise made to a foreign conqueror still bound the king. Verses 22–24 end with a tree that God plants himself.
Responsibility allows a changed future

The exiles used the proverb to say their fate was fixed by their parents. Verses 5–18 answer with three generations. A good father, a violent son, and a good grandson each stand alone. Verses 21–24 apply the same rule within one life. A person’s past does not lock his future. Verse 23 states what God wants. He would have the wicked turn and live.
Royal power becomes a funeral song

This is a funeral song sung while the royal house still stands. The lion recalls Jacob’s blessing on Judah in Genesis 49:9. The vine once grew strong branches fit for scepters (verse 11). Verse 14 says fire came from the vine’s own branch. The ruin begins inside the royal family. No branch remains that could rule. The verse says twice that this is a lament.
The elders hear a history of repeated refusal

Verse 32 exposes what the elders have in mind. They want to become like the nations around them. God says it “will not be at all.” He will not let them go. The history in this chapter turns four times on one phrase. God acted “for my name’s sake” (verses 9, 14, 22, 44). Israel’s story continues because of his name, and they do not earn it.
A foreign ruler's choice becomes part of judgment

Verse 21 lists three ways of seeking omens. Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids such practices in Israel. Yet the lot points where God has already said the sword will go. A foreign king’s superstition becomes part of the judgment. Verse 23 says the people of Jerusalem think the omen is false. Their doubt does not protect them. Verse 27 keeps the crown for a future rightful ruler.
The city's wrongs involve every level of power

Verses 25–29 go through the city by rank. Prophets, priests, and officials are charged first. Verse 29 then names “the people of the land.” Ordinary people also oppress the poor and the foreigner. No class is left out. Wrongs against the weak appear beside wrongs against holy things (verses 7–8). Verse 30 says God searched for one person to repair the wall.
The sisters represent cities and dangerous alliances

The sisters stand for two capital cities and their foreign alliances. Each was drawn to a great power’s strength and display. Verse 22 says the admired allies will return as enemies. Verse 37 states the actual charges under the picture. The cities worshiped idols and burned their own children. Verse 39 adds that they entered God’s house that same day. The harsh language is aimed at cities and their politics.
Public signs join the city's siege with private grief

Verse 16 calls Ezekiel’s wife the desire of his eyes. Verse 21 uses the same words for the temple. What she is to him, the sanctuary is to the people. His silence at her death shows what their grief will be like. The loss will be too great for the usual rites (verses 22–23). The text gives the prophet’s own cost one line in verse 18. It moves at once to the people’s question.
The neighbors face judgment for celebrating another people's loss

None of these nations is charged with idolatry here. Verse 6 charges Ammon with clapping and stamping for joy. They celebrated another people’s ruin. Each neighbor shows a different attitude. Moab denies that Judah was special (verse 8), and Edom takes revenge (verse 12). The Philistines act from long hatred (verse 15). God judged Judah, and that gave its neighbors no right to rejoice.
Tyre's expected gain becomes a warning of loss

Verse 2 gives Tyre’s reaction to Jerusalem’s fall. A trade rival is gone, so Tyre expects more business. The warning reverses that hope point by point. Verse 12 says Tyre’s own riches and goods will be taken. Its fine houses will be torn down. Verses 4 and 14 leave only bare rock for drying nets. The profit it expected from another’s loss becomes its own loss.
A trading city becomes a richly equipped ship

Verses 5–7 build the ship from the best materials of every coast. Verses 12–25 list its trade, nation by nation. The list shows how many peoples depended on this one city. Verse 13 includes human beings among the goods. Verse 27 then sinks everything in a single sentence. Wealth, wares, sailors, and soldiers go down together. The length of the list measures the size of the loss.
Royal splendor cannot make a ruler divine

Verse 2 quotes the ruler’s claim to sit in God’s seat. Verse 9 asks whether he will say so in front of his killers. Verses 16–17 trace how he fell. Much trade led to violence. Beauty lifted his heart, and splendor spoiled his wisdom. The Eden language makes him like Adam, favored and then cast out. Some Christian readers also see Satan’s fall here, but the text names Tyre’s king.
Egypt's river cannot belong to Pharaoh alone

The Nile was Egypt’s life, and verse 9 quotes Pharaoh’s claim about it. He says the river is his and that he made it. That is a creator’s claim. Verse 3 pictures him as a great river beast. Verses 6–7 add a second charge. Egypt was a reed that splintered when Israel leaned on it. Verses 14–15 leave Egypt alive and too small to be trusted again.
Egypt's strength fails across cities and allies

Verses 13–18 name Egypt’s cities from one end to the other. No region is passed over. Verse 18 ends at Tahpanhes. Judah’s refugees fled to that town with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 43:7–9). The verse says Egypt’s “yokes” will be broken there. Verses 21–25 add the picture of a broken arm. The ally Judah counted on cannot lift a sword.
A great tree warns Pharaoh about exalted power

Pharaoh hears his warning through the story of another empire. Assyria had been greater than Egypt, and it had already fallen. Verse 6 shows the tree doing good. Birds nested in it, and nations lived in its shade. Verse 10 names the fault: its heart was lifted up because of its height. Verse 14 gives the lesson for every tall tree. None should exalt itself, since all are headed for death.
The funeral song places Egypt beside fallen powers

Verse 18 sends Egypt down to join other great powers. The verses that follow read like a roll call. Each nation “caused terror in the land of the living.” Each now lies still and bears its shame. The phrase returns again and again (verses 23–27, 32). Egypt takes its place among equals. Verse 31 gives Pharaoh one comfort: he is not alone there.
Hearing the warning is different from acting on it

After Jerusalem falls, Ezekiel is proved right, and people come to him. Verse 30 shows them inviting one another to hear the word. Verse 31 says they sit, listen, and do nothing. Their mouths show love, and their hearts chase gain. Verse 32 compares the prophet to a singer with a fine voice. An audience that enjoys him has not obeyed him. Verse 33 says events will show that a prophet was among them.
The shepherd must repair harm and prevent further abuse

Verse 4 lists what the shepherds failed to do. Verse 16 takes up that list item by item. God will seek the lost, bind the injured, and strengthen the sick. The verse then adds a judgment on the fat and strong. Verses 17–22 explain it. Some sheep push the weak aside and muddy the water. Care for the hurt includes restraint of those who hurt them.
Seir's claim to the land meets God's continuing presence

After the exile, the lands of Israel and Judah looked empty. Verse 10 quotes Edom’s plan to take both. The verse then adds one clause: “although the LORD was there.” The land appeared abandoned, and its owner had not given it up. Edom’s claim ignored him. Verse 13 says Edom’s boasting was aimed at God. The next chapter speaks to those same mountains with a promise.
A restored land requires a changed people

The promise comes in a set order. God gathers the people (verse 24) and cleanses them (verse 25). Then he gives a new heart (verse 26) and his Spirit (verse 27). Obedience follows from that. A heart of stone does not respond; a heart of flesh does. Without that change a return would only repeat the past (verses 17–19). Verses 22 and 32 say he does this for his name, not their merit.
Revived bones and joined sticks answer divided hope

Verse 11 quotes what the exiles are saying. Their bones are dry, their hope is gone, and they are cut off. The vision answers that saying. It happens in two stages (verses 7–10). The bodies are formed first and have no breath. Life comes only when the breath enters, as in Genesis 2:7. The two sticks in verses 16–22 then promise one reunited people.
A secure people become the target of planned plunder

Verse 11 gives Gog’s reasoning. The villages have no walls, bars, or gates. Their people are at rest and suspect nothing. He sees their peace as an opening. Verse 13 shows traders watching for a share of the loot. Verse 16 states God’s purpose in letting him come. The nations will learn who guards a people with no walls.
The invader's weapons become fuel instead of power

Verses 9–10 turn the invaders’ weapons into firewood. Verses 12–16 turn their army into a long burial task. Tools of terror become household fuel and a cleanup job. Verse 22 gives the result for Israel: they will know the LORD. Verse 23 gives the result for the nations. They will learn that the exile came from Israel’s guilt, not God’s weakness. Verse 29 ends with his face no longer hidden.
A measured vision prepares the people to see again

Verse 1 dates this vision fourteen years after the city fell. The exiles have no temple. Verse 4 gives Ezekiel three commands: see, hear, and set his heart. Then he must report everything to Israel. The guide measures, and Ezekiel watches and records. Exact sizes make the future house solid in the hearers’ minds. Nine chapters of measurements are a form of hope.
The inner rooms give sacred space a clear order

The guide speaks very little in these chapters. Verse 4 is one of the few things he says. He names the inner room. Verse 3 notes that he “went inward” to measure it. Ezekiel is a priest, and he stays outside. The doorways grow narrower toward that room (verses 2–3). The building’s plan teaches that nearness to God has steps.
Priestly rooms protect the distinction between sacred and common

Verse 14 gives a rule about clothing. Garments worn in service stay in the holy rooms. The priests change before they go out among the people. Holiness is treated as something not to be carried about carelessly. Verse 20 states the purpose of the whole outer wall. It marks off the holy from the common. Chapter 22:26 charged the earlier priests with ignoring that difference.
The returning glory requires distance from former wrongs

The glory left by the east gate in 10:19 and 11:23. It returns by that same gate in verse 4. Verse 3 ties this sight to the earlier visions. Verse 7 says God will live here forever, and it sets a condition. The people must no longer defile his name. Verse 8 recalls kings who built beside his house with only a wall between. Verses 10–11 say the plan itself should make Israel ashamed.
Priests must teach the distinctions they once failed to keep

Chapter 22:26 accused the priests of teaching no difference between holy and common. Verse 23 answers that charge. The restored priests must teach exactly that difference. They must also help people tell clean from unclean. Verse 24 adds that they judge disputes by God’s rules. Their own habits of dress and conduct model the lesson (verses 17–22). Verse 28 says God himself is what they own.
Land and honest measures restrain royal abuse

Verses 7–8 give the prince a fixed estate with marked borders. He has his own land and no reason to take another’s. Verse 9 then speaks sharply: “Enough, you princes of Israel!” It names violence, plunder, and driving people from their homes. First Kings 21 shows a king taking Naboth’s vineyard. Verses 10–12 add honest weights and measures. Seizing land and cheating in trade are treated as one kind of wrong.
The prince's family gifts must not displace other households

Verses 16–17 limit what a prince may give away. Land given to his sons stays in his family. Land given to a servant returns in the year of release. Verse 18 states the rule beneath both. He may not take the people’s inheritance to enrich his house. The reason given is that no one be driven from his property. Verse 10 has the prince enter and leave with the people.
Life from the sanctuary reaches land shared with foreigners

The river starts as a trickle and grows with no streams joining (verses 3–5). It heals the most lifeless water in the land (verses 8–9). Verse 22 then turns to who may own the renewed land. Foreigners who live there and raise children receive a share. They are to be treated as native-born Israelites. Leviticus 19:34 told Israel to love the foreigner. This verse gives the foreigner land.
The city's final name completes the promise of presence

Joshua’s division gave the tribes uneven shares. This one gives each tribe a strip of the same kind. The northern tribes lost in exile are all present. Each tribe has a gate into the city (verses 31–34). The book began with God’s glory seen in Babylon. It showed that glory leaving Jerusalem. Verse 35 ends with a city renamed for his presence.
